title: Stress Prober and Benchmark Playbook for Dedicated Throughput SLA
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Create a reproducible, customer-facing playbook and accompanying stress-prober tool that formalizes how we measure dedicated capacity throughput for SLA guarantees. Deliverables: (1) a benchmarking playbook with workload profiles and pass/fail criteria, (2) a lightweight stress-prober harness that can run locally and in CI against dedicated pools, (3) a customer acceptance test suite for Dedicated customers to validate committed throughput during onboarding, and (4) telemetry events + dashboards to continuously validate SLA compliance.
acceptance_criteria: Playbook defines 5 canonical workload profiles (short-chat, long-chat, embeddings, batched-batch, high-concurrency burst) with sequence length distributions and target p95/p99 latency thresholds.
Stress-prober v1 runs as a containerized binary, accepts config for model, pool, qps schedule, concurrency, and KV cache priming; produces a standardized CSV of latency/throughput/error metrics.
CI pipeline integration: nightly benchmark job that runs against a non-production dedicated pool and publishes run artifacts to S3 and updates the dedicated-throughput-dashboard.
Customer acceptance suite: end-to-end script and checklist that an SE or customer can run against their reserved pool yielding a signed-off PDF report with pass/fail and observed headroom.
Dashboards ingest prober telemetry (token counts, failed requests, queue length, p95/p99) and raise an alert when observed throughput drops below 90% of committed capacity for >10 minutes.
Security review completed for prober (no credentials baked into artifacts) and product marketing has an initial one-pager for the onboarding flow.
Documentation and quickstart written in Confluence and linked from Console onboarding flow.
testing_plan: Phase 1: Local dev loop — run stress-prober against a small local docker-compose stack that simulates a 2-GPU dedicated pool (unit-level validation of qps scheduling and KV cache priming).
Phase 2: Staging benchmark — execute full workload profiles against staging dedicated pool (3 runs per profile at different time-of-day) and baseline p50/p95/p99 and throughput curves.

Phase 3: Canary / Production smoke — run minimal acceptance suite after any autoscaling policy change or runtime release on a canary dedicated pool; fail if errors or sustained latency regressions observed.
Phase 4: Customer acceptance — provide a scripted harness + checklist for customers; require two consecutive runs within 72 hours that meet pass criteria before marking onboarding complete.
Metrics collected: per-request latency (p50/p95/p99), tokens/sec, batch sizes, GPU utilization, request queue length, error types (overload, timeouts, model fallback).
